The first four rows are grouped by natural features, which the chapter lists as physiography, climate, vegetation, soil and wildlife. The remaining rows are grouped by man-made features, which the chapter lists as socio-cultural factors such as language and ethnicity, political factors such as administrative boundaries, and economic factors such as GDP.

No. The common factor tells us what the areas share, but the chapter states that every region also has four attributes: location, which can be expressed in latitudes and longitudes; spatial extent, decided on the basis of homogeneity; a boundary, beyond which another region begins; and a hierarchical arrangement into orders or sub-regions. Any of these can also be used to separate one area from another.

The chapter groups the characteristics into two kinds.

Natural (physical) characteristics: physiography, climate, vegetation, soil and wildlife. For example, the Himalayan ranges and the Northern Plains of India are separated on the basis of their altitude and topography.

Man-made characteristics: socio-cultural factors such as language and ethnicity, political factors such as administrative boundaries, and economic factors such as GDP. For example, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra are separate regions because each has its own boundary and government.

In addition, every region can be described by its location, spatial extent, boundary and hierarchical arrangement.

The identifying characteristic is the economic activity that binds the surrounding areas to a central city. The chapter gives this very example: the area under the Pune Metropolitan Region is bound by economic activities, with the periphery supplying the core with vegetables, flowers and other perishable items, and the core paying the surrounding region for those products. It is therefore a functional region.

The identifying characteristic is a central focal point that connects the areas around it. The chapter defines a functional region as an area organised to function socially and economically as a single unit, centred on a focal point that connects other areas through transportation, communication or economic activities. A hub is organised around one such centre, so it is a functional region.

The identifying characteristic is a natural physical feature, the lake itself. The chapter lists physiography, climate, vegetation, soil and wildlife as the natural features on which a region is based, and an area sharing one such physical characteristic is a formal region. The lake gives the area a homogeneous physical character and a clear boundary at the water's edge.

The identifying characteristic is a single economic activity, tourism, organised around one centre. The area is tied to that centre by the services it provides and the visitors it draws, which matches the chapter's definition of a functional region as an area organised to function socially and economically as a single unit around a focal point.

Uttar Pradesh, District Kolhapur and Taluka Haveli are administrative units with fixed boundaries; the rice-producing region of Konkan shares one crop and the black cotton soil region shares one soil type. Each is an area whose people or land share one or more characteristics in common, which is the chapter's definition of a formal region.

The other five are each organised around a focal point and defined by the area that point serves: a dam, a transport undertaking, a cable operator, a railway network and a health centre. The chapter defines a functional region as an area organised to function socially and economically as a single unit around such a focal point, and gives Wi-Fi hotspots, pizza delivery areas and milk centre areas as parallel examples.

Region A. It performs best on every indicator in the table: the highest per capita income at 15466, the lowest population below the poverty line at 14 per cent, the highest urbanisation at 45 per cent, the highest ratio of net irrigated area to total sown area at 64 per cent, and the highest per capita electricity consumption at 557 units. The chapter notes that a high per capita income indicates high production, and that a low figure generally indicates the presence of fewer resources and lesser utilisation of them.

Region A. Its per capita income of 15466 is the highest of the three, against 10432 in region B and 5000 in region C, and only 14 per cent of its population is below the poverty line against 32 per cent in B and 48 per cent in C.

Region A is the likeliest, because all five indicators point to a better life there: higher income, less poverty, more urbanisation, better irrigation and more electricity per person. The chapter draws exactly this conclusion, saying these indicators point to the fact that life in region A may be better than in the other two. It also warns that the indicators are not enough to give a complete picture, so happiness cannot be settled from this table alone.

No. The chapter states plainly that these indicators are not enough to give a complete picture of a region, and names the further indicators that would give a better one: literacy rate, enrolment ratio and dropout ratio, sex ratio, and crime rate against women and children. It adds that there are many indicators based on the social, economic, political, cultural and environmental conditions of a region.

The pattern the table is teaching is the one stated in the chapter: fertile land, favourable climate and good rainfall promote development, while a difficult physical setting holds it back even where other resources exist.

[Note: this chapter does not name the region of the coniferous forest row, and it does not state the geographical factors of the Nile basin or of Indonesia and Malaysia, nor the effects on Japan. Those cells have been completed from the pattern the chapter sets out rather than from a statement made in it.]

The countries in the later stages. The chapter states that in the five stages of Demographic Transition the later stages have low birth rates and death rates, and that regions with such low growth will have greater development because there will be less population to spend on. It adds that the quality of the population is equally important, so a late stage alone does not make a country developed.

Population and development are closely interrelated, and the chapter says all the parameters of development are measured keeping the population of a region in mind. Population density, age, sex, fertility, mortality, occupational structure, literacy rate and life expectancy together decide how much pressure falls on a region's resources and how efficiently those resources are used. A high dependency ratio forces a large amount of capital to be spent on supporting dependents, while a relatively large working-age population is associated with higher economic development and higher living standards. The relationship runs both ways: a higher population lowers per capita income, but a very low population can also hamper development because there is not enough human capital to exploit the resources.

The correlation is negative but weak, about -0.24. The negative sign means that regions which spend a larger share of their budget on education tend to have fewer malnourished children: C spends the most, 7.10 per cent, and has almost the lowest malnutrition at 3.4 per cent, while E spends the least but one, 4.09 per cent, and has the highest malnutrition at 31.7 per cent.

This matches the chapter's point that no one indicator can decide the development of a region, and that a holistic view needs the physical, economic, social and environmental aspects together.

For each region it gives the percentage of land under five categories: arable land, permanent crops, permanent meadows and pastures, forests, and other land. Alongside the land use it gives the region's GDP in billion dollars for the year 2017, so that the pattern of land use can be compared with the size of the economy.

Region C. Agricultural land is arable land together with land under permanent crops, which for C is 52.0 plus 16.0, that is 68.0 per cent. The next highest is F with 57.8 plus 0.6, that is 58.4 per cent, and then I with 50.1 plus 4.1, that is 54.2 per cent.

If only the arable land column is read, F is the highest at 57.8 per cent against C's 52.0 per cent, so it is worth saying which of the two columns is being counted.
Region I, with a GDP of 11325.66 billion dollars in 2017. That is nearly twice the next highest, region K at 5747.49 billion dollars.

Region K, with 66.0 per cent of its land under forests. Region E is next with 57.0 per cent, followed by J with 48.5 per cent.

[Note: the question asks which country has the most land under forests, but the table lists regions labelled A to L and does not name any country, so the answer can only be given as a region.]

Region G, with 95.6 per cent of its land in the 'other land' category. Its GDP is 1391.25 billion dollars.

The figure is high because almost nothing else is possible there: G has only 2.8 per cent arable land, 1.0 per cent under permanent crops, no permanent meadows and pastures at all, and 0.1 per cent under forests.

The land use pattern alone does not decide how large a region's economy is. Region I has both a large share of agricultural land, 50.1 per cent arable, and much the highest GDP at 11325.66 billion dollars, which suggests a link. But region C has the largest agricultural share of all, 68.0 per cent counting permanent crops, and a GDP of only 837.58 billion dollars, while region G has 95.6 per cent of its land in the 'other land' category and still records 1391.25 billion dollars, more than C.

What the table does show is that land use reflects the physical setting of a region, and that how a region uses its land matters more than how much of one category it has. This matches the chapter's point that the way the people of a region use their land will help the region develop faster, and that no single factor gives a holistic view of development.
Region A, where the primary sector contributes only 1 per cent of GDP.
Region E, where the primary sector contributes 14 per cent of GDP, well above region D at 6 per cent and the rest at 1 to 2 per cent.
Region B, where the tertiary sector contributes 66 per cent of GDP, just ahead of region A at 65 per cent.
Region A, with a Human Development Index of 0.93 in 2018.

Yes. The regions that depend least on primary activities and most on tertiary activities tend to have the higher Human Development Index. Region A has the smallest primary share at 1 per cent and the highest HDI at 0.93, while region E has the largest primary share at 14 per cent and the lowest HDI at 0.65.

The chapter states this directly: regions are generally developed if they contribute more in the tertiary sector and depend less on primary activities, because tertiary activities contribute more to the income of the region.

The rule is a tendency and not an exact one. Region B has the highest tertiary share of all at 66 per cent, yet its HDI of 0.85 is below region A's 0.93, and region C has a higher tertiary share than region D, 61 against 60.8 per cent, but a lower HDI, 0.71 against 0.81.

The chart divides the strategy into two branches.

**Provision of Public Goods and Services**

Provision of Drinking Water: a reliable water supply removes a daily burden that falls hardest on the poorest households. It also reduces disease, and the chapter notes that areas where water is scarce and diseases flourish will be less developed.

Education: education raises the quality of the population, which the chapter says is as important as its quantity. A better educated workforce can use a region's natural resources more efficiently, which is what the chapter calls holistic development.

Justice and Law and Order: secure conditions are what allow investment to enter a region. The chapter notes that private investment concentrates where conditions are favourable, so a region without order stays outside that flow.

Medical and Health Facilities: better health raises life expectancy, which the chapter lists among the indicators of development, and keeps the working-age population productive.

Electricity to all: per capita consumption of electricity is one of the indicators used in the chapter's own table of regional performance. Power is also a human factor the chapter names as decisive in disparity in development.

All weather roads: roads give access to markets throughout the year. The chapter lists transportation and access to markets among the human factors that have played a dominant role in disparity in development.

**Provision of Infrastructure and Stimulus**

Policy Review and Reforms: the chapter describes identifying undeveloped regions and the reasons behind their non-development, which may be physical, social or economic. Reviewing policy is how that identification is turned into action.

Special Funds: funds are allocated to the regions that need them in particular sectors, and the chapter says such funds are given in the form of subsidies and investments.

Skill Development: skilled labour is the first human factor the chapter names. Building skills locally lets a region use its own resources instead of depending on labour drawn from elsewhere.

Support to Infrastructural Projects: the chapter notes that private investment is generally concentrated in regions that already have basic infrastructural facilities, so public support for infrastructure is what breaks that circle.

Governance: sound governance decides where industries and projects are located, which the chapter says increases employment and brings other advantages for the residents there. Decentralisation of industries is named in the chapter as a strategy in its own right.

| Point of difference | Functional region | Formal region |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | Organised to function socially and economically as a single unit | Inhabited by people who have one or more characteristics in common |
| Structure | Centred on a focal point that connects the other areas | Homogeneous throughout, with no central point required |
| What ties it together | Systems such as transportation, communication or economic activities | A shared characteristic such as a common language, a particular crop, or a physical feature |
| Boundary | Set by how far the focal point's service or influence reaches | Set by how far the shared characteristic extends |
| Examples | Cities, television signal areas of a TV tower, Wi-Fi hotspots, pizza delivery areas, milk centre areas, the Pune Metropolitan Region | River basins, districts, a crop-producing region, a soil region |

| Point of difference | Physical region | Political region |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | Natural features | Man-made features |
| Defining characteristics | Physiography, climate, vegetation, soil and wildlife | Administrative boundaries and the government that runs them |
| How the boundary arises | Formed by nature, where the natural feature ends | Drawn by people, and it can be redrawn |
| Examples | River basins, the Himalayan ranges as against the Northern Plains, deserts | States such as Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, districts such as Pune and Ahmednagar, talukas |

Both are formal regions, because in each case the area is homogeneous in the characteristic that defines it. The chapter notes that the States Reorganization Act of 1956 drew state boundaries according to language after independence, which shows how a political boundary can be redrawn while a physical one cannot.

Regional development depends on several groups of factors working together, and the chapter is clear that no single one of them decides it.

Physical factors: climate and relief. Where land is less fertile, water is scarce and diseases flourish, a region will be less developed, as in the tropical rainforests. Fertile land, a favourable climate and good rainfall promote development, as in the Mediterranean region. The physical setting matters too: a landlocked region, one in high mountain ranges, or one lacking navigable rivers, long coastlines or good natural harbours may not develop well even where other resources are present.

Population: density, age, sex, fertility, mortality, occupational structure, literacy rate and life expectancy decide both the pressure on a region's resources and how efficiently they are used. A large working-age population supports higher development, while a high dependency ratio consumes capital in supporting dependents.

Land use: developed and undeveloped regions differ in the percentages of land under each use, and the chapter says the way people use their land helps a region develop faster.

Economic activities: regions are generally developed if they contribute more in the tertiary sector and depend less on primary activities.

Human and economic factors: skilled labour, technology, transportation, access to markets, communication facilities, power, banking and insurance.

The chapter sets out the measures India has used to reduce regional imbalance.

First, the regions which were not developed are identified, and the reasons behind their non-development are identified as well. These reasons may be physical, social or economic, and different types of criteria are used to identify such areas.

Second, funds are allocated to those regions which need them in particular sectors or fields, and sectorwise investments are then made to improve conditions there. These funds are given in the form of subsidies and as investments in roads, schools, agriculture, irrigation, industries, housing, and medical and health facilities.

Third, special care is taken of regions identified as drought-prone, desert, hilly or tribal-dominated.

Fourth, decentralisation of industries is used as a strategy, so that industry does not remain concentrated in the regions that already have infrastructure.

The purpose of the policy is to redress inequalities between different regions of the country and to raise the standard of living to a higher level at a uniform rate.

Because the physical setting decides what a region can do with itself. The chapter states that physical factors such as climate and relief affect a region's development: where land is less fertile, water is scarce and diseases flourish, the region will be less developed, as in the tropical rainforests, while fertile land, a favourable climate and good rainfall promote development, as in the Mediterranean region.

The setting also decides how easily a region can connect with others. If a region is landlocked, lies in high mountain ranges, or lacks navigable rivers, long coastlines or good natural harbours, it may not develop well even when other natural resources are present.

The chapter also notes the reverse case, where large resources exist but the climate is unfavourable or there is no population to exploit them, and gives Antarctica as the example.

Because development depends on the quality of a region's population, not only on its numbers. The chapter lists literacy rate among the factors that determine how efficiently the resources of a region will be used by its population, and names education among the indicators of development.

An illiterate population cannot supply the skilled labour, technology and enterprise that the chapter identifies as human factors playing a dominant role in disparity in development. Poverty works the same way: the chapter uses the percentage of population below the poverty line as an indicator of a region's performance, and a poor population has little capacity to invest in or make use of new facilities.

The two reinforce each other. Poverty keeps children out of education, and illiteracy keeps incomes low, so the region stays behind others even where resources exist.

Because the physical setting of the Himalayan region works against it on almost every count the chapter names. Physical factors such as location, relief, altitude, availability of resources and accessibility are responsible for imbalanced regional development, and a high mountain region is disadvantaged on all of them.

The chapter states directly that states located in difficult terrains surrounded by hills and dense forests, such as Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand and several north-eastern states, are behind other regions that have more mineral and other resources. Such regions are landlocked and lie in high mountain ranges, which the chapter gives as conditions under which a region may not develop well even where other resources exist.

Human factors follow from this. Transportation, access to markets and communication facilities are all harder to provide in mountainous terrain, and the chapter notes that private investment concentrates in regions that already have basic infrastructural facilities, which leaves such regions further behind.

A region is a geographical area that distinguishes itself from another area. Small or large areas of land having common features can be identified separately, and generally there is a boundary which demarcates one area from another.

The features that make a region may be natural or man-made. The natural ones are physiography, climate, vegetation, soil and wildlife; for example, the Himalayan ranges and the Northern Plains of India are treated as two regions because of their altitude and topography. The man-made ones are socio-cultural factors such as language and ethnicity, political factors such as administrative boundaries, and economic factors such as GDP; for example, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra are two regions because each has its own boundary and government.

An area which has common characteristics and is homogeneous in nature constitutes a region. In geographical studies the region is the basic unit, because it lets us differentiate one area from another.

Every region has four attributes. It has a location, which can be expressed in latitudes and longitudes. It has a spatial extent, decided on the basis of homogeneity. It has a boundary, beyond which there is another region. And it has a hierarchical arrangement, so that it can be divided into orders or sub-regions on the basis of common characteristics.

Regions can be very small or very large, and a region can contain two or more sub-regions. Within the Northern Plains of India there are the Indus and its tributaries, the Ganga-Yamuna plains and the Brahmaputra-Hooghly plains; within a district there are talukas, and each taluka, city and village is itself a region.

Regions are differentiated on the basis of their common characteristics, and the chapter divides these into natural and man-made.

Natural (physical) factors are physiography, climate, vegetation, soil and wildlife. For example, the Himalayan ranges and the Northern Plains of India are differentiated on the basis of their altitude and topography. River basins such as the Ganga, Amazon, Mississippi and Nile basins form regions on the basis of a river, and the Thar, Arabian, Gobi and Sahara form regions on the basis of desert conditions.

Man-made factors are of three kinds. Socio-cultural factors such as language and ethnicity give the Marathi-speaking and Hindi-speaking belts; the chapter notes that the States Reorganization Act of 1956 drew state boundaries according to language after independence, so that Maharashtra became the state of Marathi-speaking people and Tamilnadu the land of Tamil-speaking people. Political factors such as administrative boundaries give states like Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, districts like Pune and Ahmednagar, and talukas within them. Economic factors such as GDP distinguish regions by the size and character of their economies.

Regions are also differentiated by their attributes: location expressed in latitudes and longitudes, spatial extent, boundary, and hierarchical arrangement into sub-regions.

Finally, a region may be differentiated by how it is organised. A formal region is homogeneous in a shared characteristic, such as the rice-producing region of Konkan; a functional region is organised around a focal point, such as the area served by a TV tower or the Pune Metropolitan Region.

Per capita income is an important indicator, but it cannot by itself measure regional development.

It is an average, and an average hides how income is shared. The chapter's own table sets per capita income beside the percentage of population below the poverty line, and the two need to be read together: a region can show a respectable average while a large share of its people remain poor.

The figure is also ambiguous on its own. The chapter explains that a lower per capita income could mean either that the population is high or that total income is low, and that in general it indicates fewer resources and lesser utilisation of them. The same number can therefore describe two different situations.

Most importantly, income says nothing about the conditions in which people live. The chapter states that no one indicator can be the only factor deciding the development of a region, and that considering only one or a few factors will never give a holistic view. It names urbanisation, the ratio of net irrigated area to total sown area, and per capita electricity consumption as further indicators, and adds literacy rate, enrolment and dropout ratio, sex ratio and crime rate against women and children as ones that give a better picture. Development is considered only when the physical, economic, social and environmental aspects of a region are all taken into account.

The chapter's definition makes the point directly: regional development is the development of all regions simultaneously, raising their per capita income and living standards by exploiting their natural and human resources fully. Living standards stand beside income, not behind it.

Because ranks are repeated, a correction is added for each group of tied ranks, of (m cubed minus m) divided by 12, where m is the size of the group. There are two groups of two, each contributing (8 - 2)/12 = 0.5, so the corrected sum is 118 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 119.

rho = 1 - (6 x 119) / (12 x (144 - 1)) = 1 - 714/1716 = 0.584

Without the correction the value is 1 - 708/1716 = 0.587, so the correction makes almost no difference here.

Conclusion: the correlation is positive but only moderate, about +0.58. Regions with a larger share of land under permanent crops do tend to have a higher GDP, but the link is far from dependable. Region C has by far the largest share of permanent crops at 16.0 per cent and a GDP of only 837.58 billion dollars, while region K has just 0.8 per cent under permanent crops and the second highest GDP at 5747.49 billion dollars.

This fits what the chapter says about development: no single indicator can decide the development of a region, and considering only one or a few factors will never give a holistic view. Land under permanent crops is one influence on a region's economy, not the explanation of it.
